## F01_selection_bias — Selection bias: training pool vs official test set

**Figure 1.** The official test set is selected, not sampled. ## F02_bayesian_coverage — Bayesian baseline (E8): reliability on the official test set

**Figure 2.** The Bayesian baseline under-covers on the official test set, increasingly with the nominal level: MC-dropout (steelmanned — its hyperparameters were selected on validation coverage error) misses nominal by -0.41, -5.51 and -6.97 pp at 80/90/95% (3-seed mean), with mean 90% interval width 20.7 log-units; the deep ensemble behaves alike. ## F03_machinery_validation — Machinery validation on the exchangeable self-split (E9), both sidednesses

**Figure 3.** Machinery validation (E9) on the exchangeable self-split (n = 2,388 events, 3 seeds), where unweighted split conformal should cover at nominal. (a) Two-sided: largest |gap| 1.18 pp (GBM at 80%); the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval contains nominal in 11 of 12 cells — the exception, GBM at 95%, over-covers by 1.08 pp. (b) One-sided, learned models: largest |gap| 0.82 pp (GBM at 90%); the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval contains nominal in 9 of 9 cells. Persistence's one-sided bound is degenerate even here — coverage 0.9376 at both 80% and 90% — because a large share of its signed residuals are exactly zero (Gate 2 diagnosis); its one-sided bounds are excluded from every coverage claim. On exchangeable data a deviation in either direction indicates a defect, so exactness is a two-sided question (Figure 12). Error bars: 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals (seed-averaged).

## F04_gate2_headline — Gate 2 headline: naive vs rule-weighted two-sided coverage, and its robustness to clustering

**Figure 4.** Rule-derived weighting restores two-sided marginal coverage on the selection-biased official test set (n = 2,167). (a) At nominal 90%, naive split conformal's under-coverage is established for every base learner (interval wholly below nominal) and the rule-weighted version's is not. The pre-registered primary contrast (persistence) moves from 0.858 to 0.926 (McNemar exact p = 5.6e-45; 148 events uncovered → covered, 0 the reverse). (b) The headline is robust to clustering events by mission (18 missions): under both the iid and the mission-level cluster bootstrap, persistence's weighted interval lies wholly above nominal (lower bounds 0.9151 and 0.9087) and its naive interval wholly below. Across the 12 learner × level cells the two schemes agree in 11; the exception — GBM at 80% — is not an improvement in coverage: the weighted point estimate is below nominal under both schemes, and the cluster verdict passes only because its wider interval can no longer establish under-coverage. Verdict: RESTORED iff the naive interval's upper bound is below nominal and the weighted one's is not — the one-sided guarantee, coverage ≥ 1 − α, so over-coverage satisfies it.

## F05_one_sided_non_restoration — One-sided upper bounds: naive vs rule-weighted split conformal (learned models)

**Figure 5.** Rule-derived weighting does not restore one-sided upper-bound coverage for any learned model (official test set, n = 2,167). Under the same criterion as Figure 4: at 90% and 95% the naive bound under-covers and the weighted bound still does (6 of 9 cells: GBM 0.850 → 0.854; GBM 0.901 → 0.922; GRU 0.876 → 0.870; GRU 0.916 → 0.926; MC-dropout 0.870 → 0.866; MC-dropout 0.914 → 0.922). At 80% the naive bound shows no deficit, and the weighted bound's interval lies wholly below nominal (GBM 0.821 → 0.759; GRU 0.821 → 0.763; MC-dropout 0.809 → 0.762): there, weighting creates a one-sided deficit where there was none. The same one-sided code path covers at nominal on the exchangeable self-split (Figure 3b), so this is an effect of the shift, not of the implementation. Persistence is excluded: its one-sided bound is degenerate (Figure 3). 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals, 3 seeds.

## F06_cqr_adaptivity_and_weighting — CQR: adaptive widths, and the effect of rule-weighting on two- and one-sided coverage

**Figure 6.** Conformalized quantile regression (E12; GBM quantile heads). (a) CQR adapts: its widths vary from event to event (per-event sd 9.2 log-units at 90%) where split-conformal widths are constant, and are 4.3× narrower in the median (5.5 vs 23.6 log-units, rule-weighted; 3-seed means; the scatter shows the median seed). (b, c) Rule-derived weighting lowers CQR coverage in both arms at every level — two-sided -1.62/-0.60/-1.37 pp, one-sided -5.55/-1.43/-2.06 pp at 80%/90%/95% — and the one-sided decrease is larger at every level (one-sided: lower in 9 of 9 level × seed cells). Among the CQR arms, only one-sided CQR gains a deficit it did not have: at 80% its naive interval [0.7989, 0.8320] shows none and its weighted interval [0.7418, 0.7782] lies wholly below nominal; two-sided naive CQR already under-covers there, so weighting deepens an existing deficit. Both arms share one quantile head and differ only in the calibration quantile, and coverage is monotone in it, so lower coverage implies a lower weighted quantile; why the rule weights lower it is not claimed. The unweighted self-test covers at nominal in both sidednesses, so the machinery is not at fault. 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals, 3 seeds, n = 2,167 official-test events.

## F07_label_noise_sensitivity — Label-noise sensitivity (E14)

**Figure 7.** Label-noise sensitivity (E14): coverage when the covariance behind each reported risk is rescaled by s ∈ [0.8, 2] and the labels recomputed (s = 1 reproduces the reported labels). (a) The pre-registered primary curve — rule-weighted conformal on persistence, truly high-risk events, nominal 90% — is flat at 0.9667 at all 7 scales, in both label arms. **This flatness reflects interval width, not robustness to label noise:** persistence's 90% intervals have median width 43.4 log-units (rule-weighted GBM 23.6, CQR 5.5), and (b) the methods with narrower intervals degrade monotonically under the same perturbation — rule-weighted, GBM 0.8965 → 0.8597 (slope -0.031 per unit s, 95% CI [-0.034, -0.028], Spearman ρ = -1.00); rule-weighted CQR, GBM 0.8696 → 0.8043 (slope -0.056 per unit s, 95% CI [-0.066, -0.046], Spearman ρ = -1.00); naive, GBM 0.8369 → 0.7933 (slope -0.037 per unit s, 95% CI [-0.041, -0.033], Spearman ρ = -1.00); persistence itself drifts slightly upward: 0.9197 → 0.9368 (slope +0.013 per unit s, 95% CI [+0.011, +0.015], Spearman ρ = +1.00). Error bars: 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals, 3 seeds; descriptive, no confirmatory test.

## F08_high_risk_conditional_coverage — Marginal vs high-risk-conditional coverage (E14, s = 1)

**Figure 8.** Marginal coverage can hide subgroup failure, and here it does. At nominal 90% (s = 1, 3 seeds), coverage over all 2,167 official-test events is 0.924, 0.892, 0.857 for rule-weighted persistence, GBM and CQR respectively; conditional on the 150 truly high-risk events it is 0.467 [0.387, 0.544] for GBM and 0.200 [0.138, 0.262] for CQR (anchored labels; direct: 0.500 [0.420, 0.580] and 0.269 [0.200, 0.340]), against 0.967 [0.933, 0.993] for persistence's far wider intervals. Conformal prediction guarantees marginal, not conditional, coverage, and group-conditional claims were dropped at Gate 1 for lack of power, so the conditional shortfall is a disclosed and characterised limitation of the narrow, informative methods — a separate question from whether their marginal guarantee holds (it does for rule-weighted split conformal, Figure 4; it does not for rule-weighted CQR, Figures 6 and 11). 95% event-level percentile-bootstrap intervals (seed-averaged); descriptive, not tested against nominal.

## F09_rank_invariance — Rank invariance at a matched alert budget (E15)

**Figure 9.** Rank invariance (Proposition 1). At a matched alert budget, a bound that is a strictly increasing function of the point prediction — here, the point plus one shared conformal quantile — raises exactly the point prediction's alerts, so calibrating it cannot change the decision. Empirically, all 16 translation-class arms (split and rule-weighted conformal, one-sided and two-sided, four learners) reproduce their point prediction's alert set exactly in all 192 budget × level comparisons (hollow markers sit on the solid point markers). Only constructions that re-rank events change the decision: CQR's quantile head (GBM: 71.3 vs 113.0 missed) and E8's event-specific dispersion (MC-dropout: 101.3 vs 101.7). Persistence's ranking misses the fewest (50.0 of 150): the ranking score decides, not the calibration. Of the 20 classified methods none contradicts Proposition 1. K = 150 alerts (the official high-risk count), nominal 90%, one-sided bounds, 3 seeds, 95% event-level bootstrap intervals.

## F10_threshold_operating_curves — Threshold-rule operating curves on the extended grid, 2- and 3-day lead times

**Figure 10.** The threshold rule (alert when the score exceeds t) on the extended grid, at 2- and 3-day lead times, common population (n = 2,045 events, 138 high-risk), nominal 90%. Lines: each ranking score's full operating curve; markers: the grid thresholds (37 and 38 per horizon, 3 and 4 above t = -6); diamonds: the operational t = -6. A conformal bound that translates the point prediction moves along the point prediction's own curve (Proposition 1: P1a = P1b = P1c = 0 on all 168 translation-class rows) — calibration changes the operating point, not the curve — while CQR and the Bayesian bound trace curves of their own. Persistence is cheapest at both lead times and every cost ratio, deployable and oracle alike; the lowest deployable cost at 10:1 is persistence's point prediction at t = -6, 358 [255, 472] at 2 d and 392 [292, 500] at 3 d; every learner's best achievable (oracle) point-arm cost is higher at the longer lead time. The learned point predictions sit below the operational threshold (GBM at 2 d: 1.3 alerts at t = -6, missing 137.3 of 138), which is why the original grid, built from them, topped out at t = -6. Extending it with the bounds' own percentiles un-pinned the primary self-test read-out (26.9% of bound selections now at the grid maximum), but 69.4% of the rule-weighted read-out's bound selections still sit there: residual censoring, disclosed as a finding. Costs: 95% event-level bootstrap intervals, 3 seeds.

**Figure 11.** Where the selection-bias correction works, nominal 90%, official test set (n = 2,167, GBM base learner). ## F12_validity_vs_exactness — Two questions, two forms: validity under shift vs exactness on exchangeable data

**Figure 12.** Two questions, two forms. *Validity under shift* asks whether a method meets its guarantee, coverage ≥ 1 − α — a one-sided bound for one-sided bounds and two-sided intervals alike — so it is tested as CI upper bound ≥ nominal, and over-coverage passes. *Exactness on exchangeable data* asks whether the implementation is right: unweighted split-conformal coverage lies in [1 − α, 1 − α + 1/(n + 1)] (n = 2,391: slack 0.042 pp), so a deviation in either direction signals a defect, and it is tested as CI contains nominal. The two forms can disagree only when the interval lies wholly above nominal (first and last rows). In the first, the containment form would fail a valid, conservative method — the error found and corrected in E17's restoration criterion. In the last, the containment form correctly flags a defect (persistence's degenerate one-sided scores) that the one-sided form would pass.
